content: The ACS National Historical Chemical Landmarks Program was initiated by the American Chemical Society in 1992 and has since recognized 60 significant landmarks in the field of chemistry. This program is part of the ACS Division of the History of Chemistry and aims to create an annotated roster for chemists, chemical engineers, students, educators, historians, and travelers. 1. Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, revolutionized materials science. 2. The Chandler Chemistry Laboratory at Lehigh University in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, is a historic site of chemical research. 3. The Joseph Priestley House in Pennsylvania is the home of Joseph Priestley, who discovered oxygen. 4. Edward Morley calculated the atomic weight of oxygen, a critical advancement in chemistry. 5. Coal was identified as a source of acetyl chemicals for plastics and fibers, offering an alternative to petroleum. 6. The first nylon plant, constructed by DuPont in Seaford, Delaware, marked a milestone in synthetic fiber production. 7. The Riverside Laboratory at Universal Oil Products contributed to advancements in chemical engineering. 8. The Sohio acrylonitrile production process was a breakthrough in industrial chemistry. 9. The Houdry process enabled selective catalytic cracking of crude petroleum into gasoline. 10. Kem-Tone, a water-based latex paint developed by Sherwin-Williams chemists, transformed the paint industry. 11. The Williams-Miles History of Chemistry Collection at Harding University in Arkansas preserves significant chemical history. 12. The Hall-Héroult process, discovered independently by Charles Martin Hall and Paul Héroult in 1886, enabled the industrial production of aluminum via electrochemistry. 13. Herbert Henry Dow achieved the first electrolytic production of bromine at the Evens Mill in Midland, Michigan. 14. Gilman Hall at the University of California, Berkeley, is a historic site for chemical research. 15. Radiation chemistry was commercialized, expanding its applications in industry. 16. Thomas Willson accidentally discovered commercial processes for producing calcium carbide and acetylene in 1892. 17. The fluid bed reactor was developed for petroleum cracking in gasoline production. 18. Havemeyer Hall at Columbia University is a historic site for chemical education and research. 19. The Raman Effect, discovered by Indian physicist Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman, advanced the understanding of light scattering. 20. Synthetic rubber was developed by the United States Synthetic Rubber Program (1939–1945), crucial during World War II. 21. The development of Tagamet, a drug for treating ulcers, was achieved at SmithKline Beecham Pharmaceuticals. 22. The discovery of penicillin revolutionized medicine and saved countless lives. 23. Physostigmine, used to treat glaucoma, was first synthesized by African American chemist Percy L. Julian at DePauw University. 24. Russell Marker developed a process for synthesizing progesterone from Mexican yams, leading to the Marker degradation process and the Mexican steroid industry. 25. Hermann Staudinger laid the foundation for polymer science. 26. Polypropylene and high-density polyethylene were discovered, transforming materials science. 27. The Edgar Fahs Smith Memorial Collection at the University of Pennsylvania preserves chemical history. 28. Helium was discovered in natural gas by Hamilton Cady and David Ford McFarland at the University of Kansas in 1905. 29. Moses Gomberg isolated organic free radicals at the University of Michigan in 1900. 30. Wallace Carothers established modern polymer science. 31. Protein and nucleic acid chemistry were advanced at Rockefeller University. 32. Transcurium elements, including berkelium, californium, and others, were discovered at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. 33. Charles H. Herty, Sr., developed a method to produce quality paper from southern pine trees in 1932. 34. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has played a critical role in advancing chemical standards. 35. The commercialization of aluminum by the Pittsburgh Reduction Company (later Alcoa) in 1888 utilized Charles Martin Hall's electrochemical process. 36. The American Chemical Society was founded in 1876, with John William Draper as its first president. 37. Norbert Rillieux, an African American engineer, invented the multiple-effect evaporator, revolutionizing sugar processing. 38. Hungarian chemist Albert Szent-Györgyi discovered Vitamin C and identified it as hexuronic acid, extractable in large quantities from paprika. 39. Noyes Laboratory celebrated a century of chemistry research and education. 40. Alice Hamilton pioneered occupational medicine, improving workplace safety in America. 41. Research at the Western Regional Research Center after World War II improved the quality and stability of frozen foods. 42. The discovery of life-saving anticancer agents Camptothecin and Taxol was achieved at the Research Triangle Institute. 43. The Polymer Research Institute at the Polytechnic University of New York, established in 1946 by Herman Mark, was the first U.S. academic facility dedicated to polymer science. 44. High-performance carbon fibers were developed at the Parma Technical Center of Union Carbide Corporation. 45. Arnold Orville Beckman developed the first commercially successful electronic pH meter at Caltech. 46. The Southern Regional Research Center developed durable press and flame-retardant cotton, making it competitive with synthetic fabrics. 47. Carl and Gerty Cori's research on sugar metabolism led to the understanding of the Cori cycle. 48. George Washington Carver, born into slavery, joined Tuskegee Institute in 1896 and developed new products from peanuts and sweet potatoes while researching crop rotation and soil fertility. 49. Selman Waksman isolated antibiotics like streptomycin, the first effective treatment for tuberculosis, cholera, and typhoid fever, and neomycin, a topical antibacterial agent. 50. The Columbia dry cell battery, the first sealed dry cell battery for mass production, was developed by the National Carbon Company in 1896. 51. Neil Bartlett demonstrated the first reaction of a noble gas by combining xenon with platinum fluoride. 52. Rumford baking powder, developed by Eben Horsford, made baking easier and more reliable. 53. Tide, the first heavy-duty synthetic laundry detergent, was developed by Procter & Gamble chemists in 1946. 54. Food dehydration technology advanced food preservation. 55. The Chemical Abstracts Service has been instrumental in organizing chemical information.
